final_answer:
In a free system, the price of a good or service is determined by the interaction of two forces: the amount of the good or service that producers are willing and able to provide (supply) and the amount that consumers are willing and able to purchase (demand). When the quantity supplied matches the quantity demanded, the system reaches a balance, often called equilibrium. At this point, the price is stable because neither excess availability nor scarcity exists. If the price is too high, suppliers may produce more, but consumers may buy less, creating a surplus. If the price is too low, suppliers may reduce production, but consumers may want to buy more, leading to a shortage. Over time, these imbalances typically push the price toward equilibrium.

When a government sets a maximum price (a price ceiling), it can disrupt this balance. If the ceiling is set below the equilibrium price, suppliers may reduce production because they cannot cover their costs or earn a profit at that level. Meanwhile, consumers may try to purchase more of the good or service at the lower price, leading to a shortage. This mismatch can result in long wait times, reduced quality, or the emergence of informal arrangements to allocate the limited supply. If the ceiling is set above the equilibrium price, it has no effect because the natural price would already be lower. However, in cases of essential goods, such as housing or medicine, price ceilings can lead to significant inefficiencies and hardship.
